claims.text: On 07/01/26, the patient presented with a severe headache rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sudden 'thunderclap' onset after exertion, throbbing and diffuse, associated with mild nausea but no vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, or neck stiffness.
The patient reported no past medical history, no current medications, and no known allergies.

Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent in daily activities, works as a primary school teacher, does not smoke, consumes approximately 6 units of alcohol per week, and engages in regular jogging.
Family history is negative for cerebrovascular accidents, aneurysms, or migraines; the patient's mother has type 2 diabetes and the father has hypertension.

Initial observations on 07/01/26 recorded blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg, heart rate of 88 bpm, respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min, temperature of 36.7-36.8°C, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air.

Initial neurological examinations on 07/01/26 were unremarkable, showing the patient alert and oriented with no focal neurological deficits, normal cranial nerves, normal motor and sensory function, no neck stiffness, and unremarkable fundoscopy.
A CT head scan performed at 14:45 on 07/01/26 showed no evidence of intracranial haemorrhage or mass lesion.
Blood tests collected at 15:15 on 07/01/26 revealed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L), CRP of 8 mg/L, and normal renal and liver function tests.
On 07/01/26, the patient was admitted to the Neurology ward with a working diagnosis of Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS) and a plan to start oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours.

On 07/01/26, the patient reported persistent headache rated 7/10, with blood pressure recorded at 150/92 mmHg and new laboratory findings of mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) and marginally elevated CRP (12 mg/L).
On 07/01/26, the plan included continuing nimodipine 60 mg orally every 4 hours and adding potassium chloride 1 g orally twice daily to correct hypokalemia.
On 07/01/26 at 20:00, the patient's GP was contacted to provide an update on the admission and preliminary diagnosis of RCVS.

On 08/01/26, MRI/MRA confirmed the diagnosis of RCVS, the patient reported headache severity reduced to 5/10, blood pressure was 135/85 mmHg, and laboratory results showed CRP 12 mg/L and persistent mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L).
On 08/01/26, the medication regimen was adjusted to nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours, and the plan included repeating MRA in 48 hours and continuing potassium chloride 1 g twice daily.
On 08/01/26, the patient received education on RCVS, including the importance of avoiding triggers such as intense physical exertion, stress, triptans, and ergotamines.
On 09/01/26, the patient reported headache severity reduced to 3/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and new laboratory results from 08/01/26 showed mild hyponatremia (sodium 132 mmol/L).
On 09/01/26, the plan included increasing oral sodium intake through dietary measures, restricting excessive fluid intake, and repeating MRA in 24 hours.
On 09/01/26, the rehab team assessed the patient and noted mild residual neck stiffness with no significant functional impairments, deciding to arrange outpatient physiotherapy post-discharge.

On 10/01/26, the patient reported headache severity reduced to 2/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and the plan was to maintain nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours, continue dietary measures for hyponatremia, and repeat MRA on 11/01/26.
On 10/01/26, the patient was provided with a discharge planning booklet covering RCVS management, lifestyle modifications, and warning signs.

On 11/01/26, the patient reported headache severity of 2/10, blood pressure was 125/78 mmHg, and the plan was to continue nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours and perform a repeat MRA to confirm resolution.

On 11/01/26 at 10:30, a repeat MRA showed significant improvement in cerebral vasoconstriction, confirming the diagnosis of RCVS, and discharge was planned for 12/01/26 with outpatient neurology follow-up arranged for 4 weeks post-discharge.

On 12/01/26, the patient reported no further headaches, blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, and the plan was to discharge the patient with nimodipine 30 mg PO QDS to be tapered over 2 weeks, referral for neurology outpatient follow-up in 4 weeks, and advice to avoid known triggers.

On 12/01/26 at 12:00, the patient's GP was contacted to discuss the hospital stay, diagnosis, and discharge medication, which was documented as amlodipine 5 mg OD, with a follow-up appointment in 4 weeks.

Medication records conflict regarding the discharge regimen: note-17 on 12/01/26 documents a plan for nimodipine 30 mg PO QDS to be tapered over 2 weeks, while note-18 on 12/01/26 documents a discussion with the GP regarding discharge medication of amlodipine 5 mg OD.
